title: literary studies|landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi
text:
This article examines the dialectical relationship between landscape representation and political exile in the poetry of Su Shi (1037–1101), arguing that his successive banishments fundamentally reconfigured his poetic engagement with the natural world. Rather than treating exile as mere biographical backdrop, this study contends that displacement served as a generative aesthetic and philosophical catalyst, transforming Su Shi’s landscapes from conventional literati topoi into dynamic sites of existential negotiation and self-reconstitution.

Drawing on close readings of key works from Su Shi’s exilic periods in Huangzhou (1080–1084), Huizhou (1094–1097), and Danzhou (1097–1100), the article traces an evolving poetics of marginal space. At Huangzhou, landmark compositions such as the “Red Cliff” rhapsodies and lyrics construct a liminal terrain where historical consciousness, Daoist transcendence, and Chan Buddhist immanence converge to mediate political trauma. As Su Shi moves deeper into the Lingnan periphery, his regulated verse and occasional poems increasingly privilege micro-landscapes—vernacular flora, quotidian weather, and peripheral geography—through which he articulates a mode of “dwelling in adversity” that complicates traditional binaries of engagement and reclusion.

Situating these texts within the broader discourse of Chinese literary exile, the article demonstrates how Su Shi’s exilic gaze produces what might be termed an “aesthetics of accommodation,” wherein alien terrain is reimagined through linguistic and perceptual appropriation as habitable world. This study contributes to Song literary studies and literary geography by illuminating how political dislocation engenders not simply nostalgic lament but a radically localized, philosophically layered mode of seeing that reshapes the Chinese poetic tradition’s relationship between self and landscape.

title: agronomy|intercropping maize and soybean under drought stress
text:
The intercropping system examined here appeared to buffer maize against the yield losses typically observed under terminal drought, though this benefit was contingent on the timing and severity of water deficit. Maize grown in mixture with soybean maintained grain yields that were, on average, 18–24% higher than those of sole-cropped maize under moderate drought, a response that likely reflected both spatial partitioning of soil water and reduced evaporative losses from the intercrop canopy. Soybean, by contrast, was generally less tolerant of the competitive environment created by the taller maize companion, particularly when water stress coincided with the R1–R3 reproductive stages; pod number per plant in intercropped soybean declined by approximately 30% relative to sole soybean under the same irrigation regime. These divergent species responses suggest that the advantage of the maize–soybean intercrop under drought may arise less from mutual facilitation than from asymmetric competition that favors maize, a pattern broadly consistent with reports from sub-humid maize–legume systems, though the magnitude of the effect appears sensitive to plant density and row configuration.

The complementary use of water between the two species may partially explain the sustained maize performance. Maize, with its relatively shallow but dense fibrous root system concentrated in the upper 40 cm, could have accessed water from the same profile as soybean during early growth, yet the deeper taproot of soybean may have extracted moisture from lower horizons as the season progressed, thereby reducing the intensity of belowground competition during the critical grain-filling period. Whether this represents true niche complementarity or merely temporal avoidance remains unclear, since root observations were limited to destructive sampling at anthesis. Additionally, the possibility that soybean fixed atmospheric nitrogen that became available to maize cannot be discounted, though the low soil moisture during reproductive growth probably constrained both nodulation activity and nitrogen mineralization. The measured improvement in nitrogen uptake in intercropped maize was modest and did not consistently reach statistical significance across drought treatments, so any nitrogen-mediated benefit should be interpreted cautiously.

Several caveats limit the generality of these findings. The experiments were conducted over two growing seasons at a single location with a clay-loam soil, and the imposed drought treatments were applied at predetermined growth stages rather than in response to naturally occurring dry spells. Under field conditions, the timing of water deficit is rarely as discrete, and the interaction between intermittent stress and intercrop dynamics may differ from what was observed here. Cultivar choice also appeared to matter: the determinate soybean genotype used in this study was less able to compensate for shading and water competition than an indeterminate type might have been, and maize hybrids with more prolific root systems could intensify suppression of the companion legume. Furthermore, the absence of a severe drought treatment means that the system’s response under extreme water shortage—where competition for limited resources would presumably intensify—remains uncertain.

A final consideration is the economic interpretation of these results. While the land equivalent ratio exceeded unity in most intercrop treatments, indicating greater overall land productivity, the partial LER for soybean was frequently below 0.5 under drought, raising questions about the attractiveness of the system where soybean is the primary commodity. The intercrop might be most appropriate in regions where maize is the dominant crop and soybean is valued partly for its contribution to soil fertility or as a risk-spreading component.

Taken together, these results indicate that maize–soybean intercropping can sustain total system productivity under moderate drought, largely through the competitive dominance and stable yield of maize, but this configuration offers limited protection to soybean and may not be economically preferable where legume yields are prioritized. The approach appears most promising when water stress is mild to moderate and occurs during late vegetative or early reproductive growth, and when management practices such as reduced maize density or altered row arrangement are used to limit suppression of the legume companion.

title: education|the effects of formative assessment on secondary school mathematics
text:
The Effects of Formative Assessment on Secondary School Mathematics

Abstract

Secondary school mathematics frequently poses considerable challenges due to its cumulative and abstract nature. Formative assessment—ongoing evaluative processes designed to improve teaching and learning rather than merely judge performance—has gained prominence as an effective pedagogical strategy. This paper examines the multifaceted effects of formative assessment on secondary school mathematics education. Drawing upon educational theory and empirical evidence, it demonstrates that formative assessment enhances student engagement and motivation, facilitates personalized instruction through timely diagnostic feedback, and improves overall mathematical understanding and achievement. Nevertheless, the paper also acknowledges practical barriers, including time constraints and the need for specialized teacher training. The findings suggest that when thoughtfully implemented, formative assessment transforms mathematics classrooms into adaptive, student-centered environments that support diverse learners and foster deeper conceptual mastery.

Introduction

Secondary school mathematics serves as a critical foundation for higher education and STEM careers, yet many students struggle with anxiety and persistent conceptual gaps. Given the subject’s hierarchical nature, unresolved misconceptions in early topics can severely impede later success. Traditional summative assessment, which typically occurs at the end of instructional units, often fails to detect or remediate these difficulties in real time. In contrast, formative assessment involves the continuous monitoring of student understanding through quizzes, observations, and discussions, providing feedback that informs both teaching and learning. Rooted in the seminal theoretical frameworks of Black and Wiliam (1998), this approach shifts the classroom focus from grade collection to active knowledge construction. This paper explores how formative assessment influences secondary mathematics instruction by examining its impact on student motivation, personalized learning, and academic outcomes, while acknowledging practical implementation challenges.

Enhancing Student Engagement and Motivation

Formative assessment fundamentally transforms classroom dynamics by positioning students as active participants rather than passive recipients. In secondary mathematics, where abstract concepts such as algebra, functions, and geometry can alienate learners, regular low-stakes assessments reduce test anxiety and encourage intellectual risk-taking. Strategies such as exit tickets, think-pair-share activities, and digital polling tools prompt students to articulate their reasoning processes. This visibility of thought builds mathematical confidence and fosters a growth mindset. Furthermore, collaborative formative strategies, such as error-analysis discussions, normalize mistake-making as a natural component of mathematical discovery. When students recognize that assessments are diagnostic rather than judgmental, they become more willing to engage with challenging problems. Consequently, formative assessment cultivates an environment where effort and process are valued alongside correct answers, thereby sustaining motivation across diverse learner populations.

Facilitating Personalized Learning and Feedback

One of the most significant advantages of formative assessment lies in its capacity to generate immediate, actionable feedback. Unlike summative examinations that merely quantify performance, formative techniques allow teachers to identify specific misconceptions—such as errors in algebraic manipulation or geometric proof construction—before they become entrenched. Through tools like diagnostic questioning and student self-assessment, educators can differentiate instruction to meet individual needs. For instance, a teacher might form small groups based on real-time data from a mid-lesson checkpoint, providing targeted scaffolding to struggling learners while extending challenges to advanced students. Technology-enhanced platforms can further streamline this process by automatically analyzing student responses and visualizing class-wide trends. This responsiveness ensures that mathematical instruction remains within students’ zones of proximal development, optimizing learning trajectories for each individual.

Improving Mathematical Understanding and Achievement

Empirical evidence consistently links formative assessment to improved academic outcomes in mathematics. By embedding assessment into daily instruction, teachers help students develop metacognitive awareness of their own learning. Processes such as self-explanation and peer evaluation encourage learners to monitor their comprehension and refine problem-solving strategies. These practices align with constructivist learning theories, which emphasize that knowledge is built through active reflection and social interaction. Longitudinal studies indicate that classrooms employing regular formative practices demonstrate greater gains in standardized mathematics scores compared to those relying solely on summative measures. Moreover, formative assessment promotes deeper conceptual understanding rather than rote memorization, enabling students to transfer mathematical principles across contexts—a skill essential for advanced mathematics and real-world application.

Challenges and Implementation Considerations

Despite its benefits, integrating formative assessment into secondary mathematics presents obstacles. Time constraints within packed curricula often limit the frequency of meaningful formative activities. Additionally, some teachers lack the professional development necessary to interpret formative data or adjust instruction accordingly. There is also the risk of “formativizing” summative tests—labeling traditional quizzes as formative without utilizing the data to inform teaching. School leaders must therefore prioritize sustained professional learning communities that allow mathematics educators to share formative strategies and refine their practice collectively. Effective implementation further requires a cultural shift to move student and parent expectations away from high-stakes grading toward process-oriented learning.

Conclusion

Formative assessment represents a transformative approach to secondary school mathematics education. By enhancing engagement, enabling personalized feedback, and improving conceptual understanding, it addresses many limitations inherent in traditional assessment models. While challenges such as time limitations and the need for teacher training persist, the pedagogical benefits warrant sustained institutional commitment. As mathematics education continues to evolve toward student-centered paradigms, formative assessment stands out as an essential mechanism for fostering resilient, adaptive, and proficient mathematical thinkers. Future research should continue to explore technology-enhanced formative tools and their long-term impact on STEM participation.

title: sociology|intergenerational support among rural migrant families
text:
Methodology

This study employs a convergent mixed-methods design combining household survey data with in-depth interviews to examine the patterns, determinants, and meanings of intergenerational support among rural migrant families in China.

 Data Sources

Quantitative data come from a household survey conducted between March and September 2023 in three major labor-sending counties (in Sichuan, Henan, and Anhui provinces) and two destination cities (Shenzhen and Hangzhou). Sites were selected to capture variation in regional economic development, migration distance, and local welfare provision. The survey gathered detailed information on intra-household transfers, caregiving arrangements, and each family member's employment, income, and health. Qualitative data consist of 62 semi-structured interviews with migrant workers (n = 30), their aging parents remaining in villages (n = 22), and spouses caring for left-behind children (n = 10). Interviews, lasting 60–120 minutes, explored the motivations, negotiations, and emotional meanings attached to support exchanges. With participants' consent, interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim.

 Sample

The survey used a multistage stratified probability sampling design. Within each site, townships or urban districts were selected with probability proportional to size, followed by villages or communities and then households. Eligible households held rural *hukou* registration and included at least one member aged 16–60 who had worked outside the home county for a minimum of three months in the preceding year. The final analytic sample comprises 1,486 households, including 1,072 migrant workers and 914 parents aged 60 or older; some households contribute both generations. Among migrant respondents, 54 percent were male, the mean age was 38.6 years, and the average migration duration was 9.2 years. Interview participants were recruited from survey respondents who agreed to follow-up contact, using maximum-variation purposive sampling across gender, age, occupation, migration distance, and family structure (e.g., households with left-behind children or elderly members living alone).

 Measures

Intergenerational support is conceptualized as multidirectional and multidimensional, encompassing: (1) *financial transfers*, measured as the value of remittances sent upward to parents and downward to children during the past 12 months; (2) *instrumental support*, including hours of grandchild care and assistance with parents' activities of daily living; and (3) *emotional support*, measured by frequency of phone and video contact and a four-item closeness scale (α = .82). Key explanatory variables include migration characteristics (duration, distance, annual return visits, intention to settle in the city), socioeconomic status (income, education, housing tenure), and family structure (number and ages of children, parental health, and co-residence status).

 Analytic Strategy

Quantitative analysis proceeds in three stages. First, descriptive statistics characterize the direction, volume, and distribution of support flows. Second, because remittance values are censored at zero, Tobit models estimate the determinants of transfer intensity, while logistic regression models estimate the probability of providing any care or maintaining frequent contact; standard errors are clustered at the household and village levels. Missing data (under 5 percent on key variables) were addressed through multiple imputation by chained equations. Third, dyadic analyses using the subsample of matched migrant–parent pairs (n = 842 dyads) assess reciprocity and the congruence between reported giving and receiving.

Qualitative transcripts were analyzed thematically in NVivo 14, combining deductive codes derived from the support typology with inductive codes emerging from the data. Two researchers independently coded 20 percent of transcripts, achieving inter-coder agreement of Cohen's κ = .85; discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated using joint displays that juxtapose statistical patterns with illustrative narratives.

The study protocol was approved by the university's institutional review board. All participants provided written informed consent, and pseudonyms are used throughout.

title: archaeology|Neolithic rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze region
text:
The transition from mobile foraging to settled farming stands as one of the most profound transformations in human prehistory, and the domestication of rice in East Asia represents a pivotal chapter in this global narrative. Today rice feeds more than half of the world's population, and its cultivation underpinned the development of complex societies across monsoon Asia. Among the several regions where rice was brought under domestication, the lower Yangtze valley has emerged as a primary center of early rice exploitation and subsequent agricultural intensification. Situated within a lacustrine and wetland environment characterized by meandering rivers, marshlands and seasonally inundated soils, this region witnessed the gradual transformation of wild rice populations into domesticated forms between the early Holocene and the middle Neolithic period. Understanding the tempo and mode of this process requires integrating archaeobotanical data with settlement archaeology, paleoecological reconstruction and recent advances in ancient DNA and phytolith analysis.

Archaeological research over the past several decades has considerably refined the chronology of early rice use in the lower Yangtze. The Shangshan culture, located in the upper reaches of the valley, has yielded some of the earliest evidence for rice exploitation, with macrobotanical remains and pottery organic residues suggesting the collection and possible cultivation of rice as early as the tenth millennium BP (Zheng et al. 2007; Liu et al. 2007). By the time of the Kuahuqiao culture, roughly 8000 to 7000 BP, rice appears in greater abundance alongside a broad spectrum of wetland resources, including acorns, water chestnuts and aquatic animals (Jiang 2013; Zheng and Jiang 2007). The subsequent Hemudu and Tianluoshan occupations, dating to approximately 7000 to 6000 BP, provide the most detailed windows onto early rice cultivation in the region, preserving waterlogged deposits rich in plant remains, wooden agricultural implements and settlement features (Fuller et al. 2009; Zheng et al. 2012). Later Neolithic cultures, including Majiabang, Songze and especially Liangzhu, demonstrate the increasing centrality of rice agriculture to subsistence economies and the capacity of agricultural surpluses to support craft specialization, social stratification and monumental construction (Liu 2004; Qin 2012).

Determining whether ancient rice remains represent wild or domesticated populations has historically challenged archaeobotanists. Traditional identifications relied primarily on the morphometry of charred grains and the presence of domestic-type husk phytoliths, with domesticated rice generally exhibiting more robust grains and distinct double-peaked phytoliths (Zhao 2010; Crawford 2012). Recent microfossil studies have refined these criteria by quantifying bulliform phytolith shape and examining the proportional ratios of different silica bodies, thereby enabling the detection of incipient domestication even when grains are absent or poorly preserved (Huan et al. 2015; Deng et al. 2018). Complementary approaches, including starch grain analysis from stone tools and human dental calculus (Yang and Jiang 2010), ancient DNA studies of de-domestication genes such as sh4 and PROG1 (Choi 2019), and stable isotope analyses of human and animal remains (Hu et al. 2006), have collectively strengthened the case for a protracted and geographically variable domestication process. Nevertheless, significant disagreement persists regarding the precise threshold at which rice cultivation became morphologically and economically dominant (Fuller et al. 2007; Nasu et al. 2012).

The environmental setting of the lower Yangtze was both enabling and constraining. Holocene sea-level rise and the expansion of freshwater wetlands created extensive habitats favorable to wild rice, Oryza rufipogon, while also presenting challenges for permanent settlement (Zong et al. 2007; Innes et al. 2009). Neolithic communities responded by developing sophisticated wooden technologies, including digging sticks, spades and ploughs, and by constructing pile-dwellings and water management features to cope with fluctuating water tables (Jiang 2013). Pollen and sediment records indicate repeated openings of the landscape through burning and clearance, suggesting that anthropogenic disturbance preceded and accompanied the spread of cultivated rice (Li et al. 2012). These interventions gradually altered local ecologies, suppressing wild rice stands and promoting domesticated morphotypes adapted to managed paddy fields.

Beyond its subsistence significance, rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze has been implicated in wider debates about the emergence of social complexity in East Asia. The Liangzhu culture, often regarded as a pristine complex society, developed elaborate jade working, large-scale hydraulic engineering and ranked mortuary differentiation against a backdrop of intensive wet-rice farming (Liu 2004; Renfrew and Liu 2018). Yet the relationship between agricultural productivity and political centralization remains contested; some scholars argue that rice surpluses directly enabled elite control and labor mobilization (Qin 2012), whereas others emphasize the continued importance of fishing, hunting and exchange networks in sustaining Neolithic social life (Jiang 2013; He 2014). Similarly, questions remain about the extent to which rice agriculture spread through demographic expansion, the adoption of cultivation practices by indigenous forager communities, or the movement of crops and knowledge along riverine corridors (Silva et al. 2015; Castillo et al. 2016).

This paper examines the archaeological evidence for Neolithic rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze with the aim of reconciling competing interpretations of its timing, ecological context and social consequences. By synthesizing recently published archaeobotanical assemblages, radiometric chronologies and paleoenvironmental datasets, we evaluate the hypothesis that rice domestication occurred as a long-term co-evolutionary process rather than a rapid technological revolution. In doing so, we seek to situate the lower Yangtze trajectory within broader comparative frameworks of agricultural origins and to highlight the roles that local environmental knowledge and social organization played in shaping one of the world's most important food crops.

title: political science|electoral reform and party fragmentation in Latin America
text:
The relationship between electoral rules and party fragmentation has occupied comparative political scientists for more than half a century. The most influential early statement is Duverger's (1954) law, which holds that single-member plurality rules tend to generate two-party competition, whereas proportional representation encourages multiparty systems. Rae (1971) refined this argument by distinguishing district magnitude, electoral formula, and ballot structure, and by showing that larger district magnitudes generally increase the number of parties winning legislative seats. Cox (1997) later clarified the strategic microfoundations of these effects, demonstrating that both voters and elites coordinate around viable alternatives when electoral rules create wasted-vote incentives. These institutional propositions were formalized empirically by Taagepera and Shugart (1989), who showed that average district magnitude is one of the strongest predictors of the effective number of parliamentary parties, a measure introduced by Laakso and Taagepera (1979). Lijphart (1994) synthesized this literature, arguing that proportional electoral systems are associated not only with greater fragmentation but also with broader patterns of consensual democracy. Collectively, this classical research treats electoral systems as an exogenous cause of party-system structure and assumes a unidirectional causal arrow from rules to outcomes.

When scholars turned to Latin America, they confronted the additional complication of presidentialism. Shugart and Carey (1992) argued that the separation of executive and legislative elections complicates the mechanical and psychological effects identified by Duverger. Because presidential contests typically create a two-candidate dynamic at the national level, parties have incentives to aggregate votes around viable contenders, yet legislative fragmentation may remain high when proportional rules and federal structures encourage localized party organizations. Jones (1995) showed that legislative electoral rules strongly shape the effective number of parties in Latin American congresses, but that this effect is conditioned by presidentialism and party discipline. Mainwaring (1993) argued that Brazil's combination of federalism, presidentialism, and open-list proportional representation generated particularly extreme fragmentation, a claim developed further by Ames (2001). Mainwaring and Scully (1995) emphasized that party-system institutionalization, not merely the number of parties, determines democratic stability. Coppedge (1997) provided cross-national evidence that district magnitude is positively associated with party-system fragmentation across several Latin American cases, although the relationship varies with socioeconomic heterogeneity and federalism.

A second wave of research challenged the assumption that electoral rules are exogenous. Colomer (2004) argued that electoral systems are themselves strategic choices made by political elites who anticipate their distributional consequences. Benoit (2004) formalized this insight, demonstrating that changes in electoral rules are usually self-interested acts by parties that expect to benefit from the new rules. Geddes (1996) observed that reformers in Latin America often designed institutions to solve immediate bargaining problems, producing long-run party-system consequences that were unintended at the time. This endogeneity perspective has important implications for the region, where many countries adopted, modified, or abandoned proportional representation, mixed-member systems, and plurality rules during democratic transitions and crises. Nohlen (1998) documented the diversity of these reforms, while Payne et al. (2002) assessed their consequences for representation and governability. Hagopian (1998) showed that where parties are weakly institutionalized, reforms may fail to produce the intended consolidation because politicians adapt strategically to new incentives rather than exiting the party system.

Country-specific studies have refined these general claims. Siavelis (1997) analyzed Chile's binomial system and argued that it produced a moderate degree of fragmentation and predictable coalitions, although it also overrepresented the largest coalitions and limited voter choice. In Colombia, Crisp and Ingall (2002) found that the shift to a personal-vote, open-list system increased candidate-centered competition without necessarily reducing the effective number of parties. Mayorga (2005) examined Bolivia's adoption of a mixed-member proportional system and concluded that it neither consolidated the party system nor prevented its subsequent fragmentation. These studies suggest that the effect of electoral reform depends on how it interacts with preexisting party organizations, federal structures, and the sequencing of presidential and legislative elections.

Despite this rich literature, several gaps remain. Much of the quantitative work relies on district-level or national-level measures of fragmentation, which may obscure how reforms alter the internal cohesion of parties, the balance between national and regional parties, or the representation of women and minorities. Moreover, the endogeneity of electoral reform complicates causal inference: reforms are often adopted during moments of crisis or transition, making it difficult to isolate the independent effect of rules from the political conditions that produced them. Future research would benefit from adopting mixed-methods designs that combine cross-national statistical analysis with detailed process tracing of reform episodes. By doing so, scholars can better specify the conditions under which electoral reform reduces, sustains, or even exacerbates party fragmentation in Latin America.

title: law|data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms
text:
The preceding analysis suggests that the current allocation of data protection responsibilities across jurisdictions creates a structurally unstable compliance environment for cross-border e-commerce platforms. Rather than operating under a coherent transnational framework, platforms appear to navigate a patchwork of extraterritorial claims, each grounded in fundamentally divergent conceptualizations of personal data. The examination of enforcement patterns indicates that the GDPR’s Article 3(2) territorial scope, while nominally clear, generates significant ambiguity when applied to marketplace operators that lack an EU establishment but actively profile Union consumers. Conversely, the sectoral approach predominant in the United States leaves contractual gaps that platforms exploit through choice-of-law clauses, particularly in disputes involving consumer biometric and geolocation data. Chinese data localization requirements, meanwhile, impose de facto fragmentation obligations that appear incompatible with the free flow commitments embedded in recent digital trade agreements. These tensions probably cannot be resolved through standard contractual clauses alone; the empirical evidence reviewed here points to persistent implementation failures where platforms treat SCCs as formalistic check-box exercises rather than operational safeguards, especially where downstream vendors operate in jurisdictions without adequacy findings.

A particularly constrained finding concerns the distinction between data controller and processor status in platform-to-seller relationships. The case law examined suggests that courts remain reluctant to classify e-commerce marketplaces as joint controllers with third-party merchants, even where algorithmic curation determines the visibility, pricing, and terms of data collection. This reluctance arguably shields platforms from direct liability under several regulatory regimes, yet it simultaneously undermines the data subject access rights that those regimes purport to guarantee. The mismatch between architectural control and legal accountability appears to be widening as platforms integrate AI-driven recommendation systems that rely on inferred rather than expressly provided user characteristics. Whether existing liability frameworks can accommodate this shift remains uncertain; the limited jurisprudence available offers only fragmentary guidance, and regulatory guidance documents have stopped short of addressing machine-inferred data categories with any precision.

Furthermore, the analysis reveals that mutual legal assistance treaties and bilateral enforcement memoranda provide inadequate scaffolding for cross-border regulatory cooperation in this sector. Enforcement asymmetries are pronounced: while EU supervisory authorities have demonstrated willingness to impose administrative fines on non-EU platforms, the practical collection of such penalties often stalls against corporate restructuring and asset localization strategies. Simultaneously, private redress avenues—including collective actions for data breaches—remain underdeveloped in several major platform home jurisdictions, suggesting that affected consumers may face a remedial vacuum even where substantive violations are well-documented. These coordination deficits are amplified by conflicting private international law rules on applicable law and forum selection, which permit platforms to fragment litigation across territories.

Limitations of this analysis should be acknowledged. The study focuses primarily on comparative assessments of the EU, PRC, and US federal frameworks, and thus may not capture the nuanced obligations emerging in Southeast Asian or African jurisdictions that increasingly host platform operations. Additionally, the rapid evolution of bilateral digital trade negotiations means that certain conclusions regarding cross-border data flows rest on regulatory proposals that have not yet achieved full legal effect. The reliance on publicly available enforcement decisions and platform transparency reports also introduces a selection bias toward high-visibility cases, potentially obscuring routine compliance practices among mid-sized operators that lack the legal resources of dominant firms. Finally, the article does not purport to offer an exhaustive treatment of technical cybersecurity standards, which intersect with, but remain analytically distinct from, data protection law proper.

Moving forward, the evidence cautions against presuming that horizontal harmonization is either imminent or necessarily desirable. Instead, a more plausible path may lie in strengthened intermediary accountability mechanisms that tether data protection obligations to specific platform functions—payment processing, algorithmic matching, logistics integration, and post-transaction dispute resolution—rather than to nominal corporate form. Such functional segmentation could mitigate some of the jurisdictional collisions identified here without requiring states to abandon divergent substantive norms. Yet this approach carries its own risks; functional tests may prove administratively burdensome for regulators with limited technical capacity and could invite regulatory arbitrage if definitional boundaries are not tightly drawn. Preliminary indications from the Digital Services Act’s conditional liability regime suggest that function-based duties are workable, though their transferability to data protection contexts remains largely untested.

The broader implication is that cross-border e-commerce governance currently occupies an uncomfortable space between trade liberalization and fundamental rights protection. Platforms are increasingly pressed to act as privatized data governance actors, yet the legal instruments available to them remain tethered to territorial sovereigns with incompatible enforcement priorities. The persistent friction between market access commitments and data sovereignty claims implies that platforms will likely continue to bear the costs of regulatory fragmentation. The findings outlined above suggest that meaningful protection for transnational consumers probably depends less on perfect doctrinal coherence than on the development of interoperable due diligence standards that can accommodate plural regulatory endpoints without collapsing into lowest-common-denominator practice. Whether such standards will emerge through multilateral negotiation, regional bloc arrangements, or private ordering remains, at this stage, an open question that subsequent empirical work must track closely.

title: religious studies|pilgrimage networks in medieval Japanese Buddhism
text:
以下是一篇约900词的课程论文初稿，结构包含摘要、引言、三个正文小节和结论，文末附真实可查的参考文献供你核实后使用。

---

 Pilgrimage Networks in Medieval Japanese Buddhism

 Abstract

This paper examines Buddhist pilgrimage in medieval Japan (c. 1185–1600) as a network phenomenon rather than an isolated devotional act. It argues that pilgrimage routes constituted connective systems linking sacred geography, monastic institutions, itinerant holy men, and lay communities, thereby enabling the circulation of doctrines, resources, and sacred authority across the archipelago. Through three case studies—the Kannon temple circuits, the syncretic Kumano region, and the itinerant fundraisers and preachers who animated these routes—the paper demonstrates that pilgrimage networks were central to the medieval transformation of Japanese Buddhism, facilitating both the dissemination of new movements and the gradual democratization of religious participation beyond court and cloister.

 Introduction

The medieval period of Japanese history, conventionally dated from the establishment of the Kamakura shogunate in 1185 to the late sixteenth century, was an era of profound religious ferment. Widespread belief in *mappō*, the degenerate final age of the Dharma, lent urgency to the search for salvation, while the rise of warrior rule destabilized the old alliance between court aristocracy and established temples. Within this context, pilgrimage (*junrei*)—journeys to mountains, temples, and shrines deemed especially efficacious—underwent a decisive transformation. Whereas Heian-period pilgrimage had been largely an aristocratic pursuit, medieval pilgrimage expanded across social classes and regions, generating durable networks of routes, inns, guides, confraternities, and sacred legends. This paper argues that these networks functioned as the connective tissue of medieval Japanese Buddhism: they distributed new teachings, financed institutions, and mapped cosmology onto the landscape. Examining the Kannon circuits, the Kumano pilgrimage zone, and the mobile religious specialists who linked them reveals pilgrimage as infrastructure—religious, economic, and social alike.

 Mapping the Sacred: Kannon Circuits and Pilgrimage Geography

A hallmark of medieval pilgrimage was the systematization of temples into numbered circuits. The most influential was the Saigoku Sanjūsan-kasho, a circuit of thirty-three temples dedicated to the bodhisattva Kannon in the Kyoto–Nara region, whose structure drew on the Lotus Sutra's account of Kannon appearing in thirty-three manifestations to save sentient beings. Legend credited the circuit to the eighth-century monk Tokudō Shōnin and its revival to the retired emperor Kazan, a paradigmatic aristocratic pilgrim. Parallel circuits emerged in eastern Japan—the Bandō thirty-three Kannon temples of the Kantō region and the thirty-four of Chichibu—so that completing all one hundred became an ideal. Meanwhile, on Shikoku, devotion to Kūkai (Kōbō Daishi, 774–835), founder of the Shingon school, generated a circuit of eighty-eight sites retracing his legendary footsteps. Such circuits performed crucial religious work. Temple origin tales (*engi*) and miracle stories (*setsuwa*) wove individual sites into a coherent sacred geography, effectively mapping buddhas' pure lands onto Japanese soil—what D. Max Moerman calls the "localization of paradise." Pilgrims did not merely travel through space; they traversed a doctrinal landscape in which each stage promised karmic merit (*kechien*) and glimpses of salvation.

 Kumano: Syncretism and the Pilgrimage of Pure Lands

If the Kannon circuits organized the sacred along routes, Kumano concentrated it in place. The three grand shrines of Hongū, Nachi, and Hayatama, deep in the Kii peninsula, exemplified *honji suijaku*, the medieval theory that local kami were manifestations of buddhas and bodhisattvas. Kumano's deities were identified with Amida, Kannon, and Yakushi, and the landscape itself was read as a mandala: Nachi's waterfall as Kannon's realm, the Hongū precinct as Amida's Pure Land. From the late Heian into the medieval period, retired emperors such as Go-Shirakawa—who reportedly undertook the journey thirty-four times—made Kumano pilgrimage a court institution, and warriors and commoners soon followed along routes lined with subsidiary shrines (*ōji*). Kumano also illustrates the era's exclusions and accommodations. As a mountain governed by *nyonin kinsei* (prohibitions on women), it restricted female access, yet women engaged its cult through boundary shrines, confraternities, and, above all, the Kumano *bikuni*: itinerant nuns who traveled the provinces with painted mandalas, preaching the shrines' virtues and soliciting donations. Kumano thus functioned simultaneously as destination and broadcast center, its sacred power disseminated outward through preaching networks.

 Holy Men, Fundraisers, and the Infrastructure of Devotion

Medieval pilgrimage networks depended on human mediators. Itinerant ascetics (*hijiri*), heirs to figures like Kūya and Gyōki, traveled between sites preaching, performing austerities, and forming karmic bonds with lay supporters. Fundraising monks (*kanjin hijiri*) turned these networks toward institutional ends: Chōgen (1121–1206), commissioned to rebuild Tōdaiji after its destruction in 1180, spent decades traversing western Japan collecting donations, converting pilgrimage circuits into channels of material support. The Pure Land preacher Ippen (1239–1289) likewise journeyed from shrine to shrine distributing paper slips inscribed with the nembutsu, his dancing congregations spreading Amidist practice along established routes. Around such travelers a durable infrastructure crystallized. Shrine agents (*oshi*) maintained client registers, offered lodging, and dispatched proselytizers; mountain guides (*sendatsu*) shepherded ascetic confraternities through sites like Ōmine, the Shugendō heartland; and village confraternities (*kō*) pooled funds to sponsor representative pilgrims, binding remote communities to distant sacred centers. Inns, ferries, and markets followed. Pilgrimage, in short, was an economy as much as a piety—one that carried medieval Buddhism's new movements into every province.

 Conclusion

In medieval Japan, pilgrimage was never simply the journey of an individual believer. It was a network: a woven fabric of routes, circuits, shrines, preachers, patrons, and institutions through which sacred power, doctrine, and wealth flowed. The numbered Kannon circuits translated scripture into geography; Kumano fused buddhas and kami into a walkable mandala; and *hijiri*, fundraising monks, and confraternities animated these landscapes, extending participation to warriors, peasants, and women otherwise barred from monastic life. By democratizing access to sacred sites while financing the temples that claimed them, pilgrimage networks helped shape the distinctly medieval character of Japanese Buddhism—popular, syncretic, and in motion—and laid foundations for the mass pilgrimages of the early modern era.
